analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Dodd-Frank law that regulates Wall Street and protects financial consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal Dodd-Frank was introduced by a single House member, drew no cosponsors, was referred to eight committees, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 in its entirety, the law passed after the 2008 financial crisis. Dodd-Frank created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, required large banks to hold more capital so they could fail without a taxpayer bailout, regulated derivatives trading, and put rules in place against the practices that contributed to the crisis. Repeal would have restored the legal landscape to pre-2008 conditions, reviving the older statutes Dodd-Frank had amended [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks, securities firms, and derivatives dealers would gain the most: the bill removes capital requirements, trading restrictions, and oversight of complex financial products, restoring the pre-2008 rules under which those businesses operated. Financial companies that consumer regulation restrains, from debt collectors to credit rating agencies, would also see obligations removed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Dodd-Frank wholesale, one short section, and revives the prior law as if the Act had never been enacted [S2] [S3].
That would lift post-crisis requirements on banks' capital, derivatives trading, and consumer-facing practices, returning regulation to pre-2008 rules [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers and taxpayers would bear the risk: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, higher bank capital cushions designed to prevent bailouts, and derivatives safeguards would all disappear, leaving households with less protection against the lending and trading practices that preceded the 2008 crisis.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would have eliminated the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the post-crisis bank rules in a single stroke, with no replacement framework [S2] [S3].

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill was that Dodd-Frank's compliance burden falls heavily on smaller banks and credit unions, which bear many of the same fixed regulatory costs as the biggest institutions; but this bill offered no targeted relief, only full repeal, which would have removed consumer and systemic safeguards along with the paperwork [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs outweighed the benefits. Whatever weight Dodd-Frank's regulatory burden carries, the bill's approach was total repeal with nothing in its place, removing consumer protections and bank-failure safeguards together with compliance costs. The bill drew no cosponsors, which suggests even most of the sponsor's own party did not treat full repeal as a workable position.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by one member with zero cosponsors, sent to eight committees, never taken up by any of them, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Adrian Smith introduced the bill on January 6, 2015, the opening day of the 114th Congress [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to eight committees, with Financial Services as the lead, and it was also referred to two subcommittees [S1] [S5].
No committee took up the bill, no hearing or markup is recorded, and no floor vote ever occurred; the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and taxpayers are better off because the bill never advanced: the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, post-crisis capital rules, and derivatives oversight remained in place. Large banks would have been the beneficiary had it passed, but they did not need this bill to win deregulatory changes during this period.

for.name: Rep. Adrian Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Dodd-Frank in its entirety; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the last recorded action was a subcommittee referral on January 26, 2015.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the bill never divided along party lines; its sole support was its single Republican sponsor [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Full repeal would have removed the capital cushions, trading restrictions, and resolution-planning rules that apply to the biggest institutions, restoring the pre-2008 rules. Their gain would come at the cost of the public's protection against bank failures and bailouts.
Dodd-Frank brought swap trading out of the shadows with clearing and reporting requirements; repeal would have returned derivatives to unregulated over-the-counter contracts.

industries.industry: Consumer financial services (debt collection, credit reporting, payday lending)
industries.note: The bill would abolish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the agency that polices these firms' treatment of borrowers, leaving consumers with the weaker pre-2010 enforcement landscape.
Dodd-Frank imposed new accountability on rating agencies whose inflated ratings fueled the crisis; repeal would have stripped that liability.
